items.followUp: State two disadvantages of star topology.

rubric.why: Identifies that the central device is critical and its failure can disrupt the network.
rubric.description: Central device is a single point of failure.
rubric.how: Award for noting that failure of the hub or switch can stop communication across the network.

rubric.why: States the advantage of expanding the network by connecting another device to the hub.
rubric.description: Easy to add or remove devices.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that devices can be added or removed easily, generally without affecting other devices.

modelAnswer: Each device is connected to a central hub or switch, so a failed cable or device usually does not affect the others.
New devices can be added or removed easily by connecting them to the hub or switch.
FollowUp: State two disadvantages of star topology.

items.followUp: Write the names of the four layers of the TCP/IP model.

rubric.description: Any two correct layer names.
rubric.how: Award one mark for correctly naming at least two layers.

rubric.why: Names the remaining layers of the TCP/IP model.
rubric.description: The other two correct layer names.
rubric.how: Award one mark for correctly naming the remaining layers; accept Link for Network Access.

modelAnswer: Application layer
Transport layer
Internet layer
Network Access layer (also called Link layer)
FollowUp: Write the names of the four layers of the TCP/IP model.

items.followUp: Give one example of an ordered list and one example of an unordered list in HTML.

rubric.why: Identifies the numbering or sequence used by an ordered list.
rubric.description: Ordered list uses numbers or another ordered sequence.
rubric.how: Award for stating that an ordered list displays items in a numbered or sequential form.

rubric.why: Identifies the bullet markers used by an unordered list.
rubric.description: Unordered list uses bullets and has no numbered sequence.
rubric.how: Award for stating that an unordered list displays items with bullets rather than numbers.

modelAnswer: An ordered list uses a sequence, usually numbers, to mark its items; in HTML it is made with the <ol> tag.
An unordered list uses bullets to mark its items; in HTML it is made with the <ul> tag.
FollowUp: Give one example of an ordered list and one example of an unordered list in HTML.

items.followUp: Draw and label the flowchart symbols for input/output and decision, and state their uses.

rubric.why: Defines a flowchart as a graphical representation of a process or algorithm using standard symbols.
rubric.description: Definition of a flowchart.
rubric.how: Award for describing it as a diagram or graphical representation of the steps in a process or algorithm.

rubric.why: Gives the terminal symbol and its use.
rubric.description: Terminal symbol represents start or end.
rubric.how: Award for naming the oval/terminal symbol and stating that it shows start or end.

rubric.why: Gives the process symbol and its use.
rubric.description: Rectangle represents a process or instruction.
rubric.how: Award for naming the rectangle and stating that it represents processing or an instruction.

rubric.why: Shows other standard symbols with their meanings.
rubric.description: Decision, input/output, and flow-line symbols.
rubric.how: Award for correctly naming and describing at least two of these: diamond for decision, parallelogram for input/output, arrow for direction of flow.

modelAnswer: A flowchart is a graphical representation of the steps of an algorithm or process using standard symbols connected by flow lines.
Oval (terminal): shows the start or end of the flowchart.
Rectangle (process): shows a processing step or instruction.
Parallelogram (input/output): shows data input or output.
Diamond (decision): shows a condition or decision, usually with Yes/No branches.
Arrow (flow line): shows the direction in which the steps are followed.
FollowUp: Draw and label the flowchart symbols for input/output and decision, and state their uses.

items.followUp: Write a note on file sharing in a computer network.

rubric.why: Defines application sharing as making software available to users over a network.
rubric.description: Meaning of application sharing.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that network users share or access applications through the network.

rubric.why: Explains that an application can be stored or run on a network computer/server and accessed by other users.
rubric.description: How users access the shared application.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning access to an application from a server or another computer.

rubric.why: States a practical benefit such as reduced software, installation, or storage costs.
rubric.description: Benefit of sharing applications.
rubric.how: Award for one valid benefit, such as reducing the need to install or store the application on every computer.

rubric.why: States that central management can make updating or maintaining the software easier.
rubric.description: Centralized management benefit.
rubric.how: Award for noting that an application can be updated or maintained centrally.

modelAnswer: Application sharing means making an application available to users through a computer network.
The application may be stored on a server or another computer and accessed by authorized users on the network.
It can reduce the need to install and store the same application on every computer, saving time and cost.
Updates and maintenance can be managed centrally.
FollowUp: Write a note on file sharing in a computer network.

items.followUp: Explain how a home network can share one Internet connection among several computers.

rubric.why: Defines Internet connection sharing as allowing several computers to use one Internet connection.
rubric.description: Meaning of Internet connection sharing.
rubric.how: Award for stating that multiple networked computers can share a single Internet connection.

rubric.why: Identifies a router or host computer as the device that provides or manages the shared connection.
rubric.description: Device used to share the connection.
rubric.how: Award for naming a router, gateway, or suitably configured host computer.

rubric.why: Explains that the computers are connected through a network to access the connection.
rubric.description: Network connection between computers.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the computers are connected together, for example through a LAN.

rubric.why: States the benefit of sharing one subscription or connection instead of separate connections.
rubric.description: Benefit of sharing the Internet connection.
rubric.how: Award for noting reduced cost or avoiding the need for a separate Internet connection for each computer.

modelAnswer: Internet connection sharing allows several computers on a network to use one Internet connection.
A router or a computer configured as a host/gateway connects the local network to the Internet.
The other computers access the Internet through this router or host over the network.
This avoids needing a separate Internet connection for every computer and can reduce cost.
FollowUp: Explain how a home network can share one Internet connection among several computers.

items.followUp: What is meant by problem definition in problem solving?

rubric.why: Explains that problem analysis involves understanding and examining the problem before solving it.
rubric.description: Understanding and examining the problem.
rubric.how: Award for stating that the problem is studied or clarified before a solution is designed.

rubric.why: Identifies the information required and the result expected as part of the analysis.
rubric.description: Determines inputs and expected outputs.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning the identification of input data and the required output; processing steps may also be mentioned.

modelAnswer: Problem analysis is the process of understanding and examining a problem before designing its solution.
It identifies the required input data, the processing needed, and the expected output.
FollowUp: What is meant by problem definition in problem solving?
